name: Esperanto
note: Spelling is regular and stress always falls on the second-to-last syllable

alphabet.e: ts, as in cats -- never the k sound
w, and only after a or e: aŭ, eŭ
g, as in go -- never as in gem
rolled with the tip of the tongue

units.title: BASICS
units.subtitle: Greet people, name who is who, and count to ten

tips.h: Word endings name the part of speech
tips.b: An Esperanto word ends in a letter that states its class: -o marks a noun, -a an adjective, -e an adverb, -i a verb in the dictionary form. One root takes any of them, so a single root learned is four words.
A greeting appears with -n because it is the object of an unspoken verb: saluton stands for mi diras saluton, I say a greeting. The plain noun saluto also exists and means a greeting.
Every letter has one sound and every letter is pronounced. No letter is silent and none changes value beside another. Stress falls on the second-to-last syllable of every word, without exception.
A plural noun adds -j after the -o ending: viro, viroj. An adjective standing with it takes -j as well, so both words show the plural.
Esperanto has one definite article, la. It never changes for gender, number or case. There is no indefinite article, so viro means both man and a man.
The pronouns are mi, vi, li, ŝi, ĝi, ni and ili. The one form vi covers singular and plural alike. ĝi stands for a thing or an animal, and for a child whose sex is not stated.

tips.h: ĉu turns a statement into a question
tips.b: A question answered by yes or no is made by putting ĉu at the front of the statement. Nothing else moves and no verb changes form. The answer is jes or ne.
ne before a verb denies the whole sentence; before any other word it denies only that word. Standing alone it answers a question.

tips.h: -e makes an adverb from any root
tips.b: The ending -e forms an adverb exactly as -o forms a noun and -a an adjective. bona is good and bone is well; certa is certain and certe is certainly.
The numerals unu through dek never change: they take no plural -j and no accusative -n. The noun counted carries the plural instead.
Numbers above ten are built from the same ten roots. A multiple of ten joins into one word and a sum stays two words, so dek unu is eleven and dudek is twenty.

units.title: EVERYDAY
units.subtitle: Food, drink, colour and the people of a household

tips.b: A verb in the present tense ends in -as whatever its subject: mi manĝas, ŝi manĝas, ili manĝas. The dictionary form of the same verb ends in -i.
The noun that receives the action adds -n, while the subject stays plain: mi manĝas panon. A plural object carries both endings and becomes -ojn.
The suffix -aĵ- turns a root into a thing made of it or produced by it: manĝi to eat gives manĝaĵo food, nova new gives novaĵo a piece of news.
Because -n marks the object, the words of a sentence may stand in any order without changing who does what. La knabo trinkas sukon and Sukon trinkas la knabo state the same fact.
A container names what it holds with da: glaso da akvo, a glass of water. With de it names the kind of vessel instead, so glaso de vino is a wine glass whether or not it is full.
The prefix mal- makes the exact opposite of a root: hela bright gives malhela dark, granda big gives malgranda small. It supplies one half of most opposed pairs in the language.
An adjective takes -j when its noun is plural and -n when its noun is an object, in that order: ruĝajn pomojn. It agrees whether it stands before or after the noun.
The suffix -in- placed before the ending gives the female of a root: patro father, patrino mother; frato brother, fratino sister. The bare root names the male or, in current use, either.
The prefix ge- names a group containing both sexes and is used with the plural: gepatroj parents, gefratoj siblings, geknaboj boys and girls.
A possessive is the personal pronoun with the adjective ending -a: mia my, via your, lia his, ŝia her, nia our, ilia their. It agrees like any other adjective.

units.title: ACTIONS
units.subtitle: The tenses, describing things, asking a question and denying

tips.h: One ending per tense, no persons
tips.b: A verb has one form per tense and it never changes for person or number: -as for the present, -is for the past, -os for the future. mi estas, ni estas and ili estas share the same word.
The infinitive ends in -i and carries no tense of its own. It follows another verb directly, with no linking word between them.

tips.h: esti links, it does not act
tips.b: esti joins a subject to a noun or an adjective. What follows it takes no -n, because nothing receives an action: Li estas knabo, La pano estas nova.
pli before an adjective means more and plej means most. The thing compared against follows ol, and the superlative takes la: la plej granda domo.
The suffix -eg- makes a root extreme and -et- makes it slight: granda big gives grandega enormous, domo house gives dometo cottage. Both attach to any root at all.
An adjective may precede or follow its noun with no change of meaning: granda domo and domo granda. It agrees in number and case wherever it stands.

phrases.t: Ŝi estas pli juna ol mi
phrases.e: She is younger than I am
phrases.ipa: ʃi ˈes.tas pli ˈju.na ol mi

tips.b: Question words begin with ki- and end in a letter naming the category asked about: -o a thing, -u a person or a choice, -a a kind, -e a place, -am a time, -al a reason, -el a manner, -om an amount, -es a possessor.
kiu and kio behave like nouns: they add -n when they are the object, and kiu adds -j in the plural. kia takes the full set of adjective endings.
A sentence beginning with a ki- word does not also take ĉu. ĉu marks only the question that is answered by jes or ne.

phrases.e: How much water do you drink?

tips.b: A neni- word already negates the sentence, so ne is not added beside it: Mi vidas nenion means I see nothing. Two negatives in one clause cancel each other out.
The neni- series takes the same final letters as the ki- series, with the same meanings: kio and nenio, kiu and neniu, kie and nenie, kiam and neniam.
mal- is not restricted to adjectives. It reverses verbs and adverbs as readily: bone well gives malbone badly, pli more gives malpli less, fermi to close gives malfermi to open.

units.title: AT HOME
units.subtitle: The house, what stands in it, what people wear and keep

tips.h: -ej- names the place for a root
tips.b: The suffix -ej- makes the place where the root happens: kuiri to cook gives kuirejo kitchen, lerni to learn gives lernejo school, dormi to sleep gives dormejo dormitory.
Two roots join into one word and the last one carries the ending and the main meaning: dormoĉambro is a sleeping room. An -o is kept between the roots where it helps pronunciation.

tips.h: -il- names the tool for a root
tips.b: The suffix -il- makes the instrument that performs the action: tranĉi to cut gives tranĉilo knife, ŝlosi to lock gives ŝlosilo key, kombi to comb gives kombilo comb.

tips.h: Suffixes stack outward from the root
tips.b: Several suffixes may follow one root, and each is read outward from it: manĝ-il-ar-o is the set of eating tools, cutlery. The last ending states the part of speech.

phrases.t: La libro estas sur la tablo
phrases.e: The book is on the table
phrases.ipa: la ˈli.bro ˈes.tas sur la ˈta.blo

tips.b: A noun after a preposition keeps its plain -o form: en la domo, sur la tablo, kun amiko. The accusative appears after a preposition for one reason only, to show movement toward.
en la domo is inside the house and en la domon is into it. The accusative added after a preposition of place turns a location into a destination.
eg: en la domo / en la domon
in the house / into the house
sur la tablo / sur la tablon
on the table / onto the table

phrases.e: The girl wears a red dress
He wears a coat and gloves

tips.b: The suffix -id- makes the offspring of a root: hundo dog gives hundido puppy, kato gives katido kitten, ŝafo sheep gives ŝafido lamb.
An animal root names the species without regard to sex. vir- prefixed marks the male and -in- the female: koko chicken, virkoko rooster, kokino hen.
The suffix -ar- makes a collection of the root: arbo tree gives arbaro forest, ŝafo gives ŝafaro flock, vorto word gives vortaro dictionary.

phrases.e: I have a dog and a cat
The horse is a big animal

units.title: TIME
units.subtitle: The week, the calendar, the clock and the weather

tips.b: The ti- series answers the ki- series letter for letter: tio that thing, tiu that one, tie there, tiam then, tial therefore, tiel so, tiom that much. The particle ĉi added to any of them makes it near instead of far.
A time noun takes -e to say when something happens: lundo Monday gives lunde on Mondays, dimanĉo gives dimanĉe on Sundays. hodiaŭ, hieraŭ and morgaŭ are already adverbs and take no ending.
The days of the week are ordinary nouns written in lower case: lundo, mardo, merkredo. They take -n and -j like any other noun.
The year is jaro and the month is monato. The twelve month names are ordinary nouns written in lower case, and en before one says in that month: en januaro.
A numeral takes -a to become an ordinal: unu one gives unua first, du gives dua second, ok gives oka eighth. A date names the day with an ordinal after la.
The letter c always stands for the sound ts, as in decembro and centro. It never carries the k sound it has in some English words.

phrases.t: La jaro havas dek du monatojn
phrases.ipa: la ˈja.ro ˈha.vas dek du mo.ˈna.tojn

tips.b: The hour is named with estas la and an ordinal: estas la tria, it is three o'clock. Minutes follow with kaj, and je states the time at which something happens.

tips.h: -e turns a time noun into when
tips.b: A part of the day takes -e to say when an action falls: mateno morning gives matene in the morning, vespero gives vespere in the evening, nokto gives nokte at night.

phrases.e: In the morning I drink coffee
He came late in the evening

tips.b: A verb of weather stands alone with nothing before it: pluvas it is raining, neĝas it is snowing, ventas it is windy. The English it has no counterpart here.

tips.h: Adverb, not adjective, for the air
tips.b: estas varma describes a named thing and agrees with it. With no noun to agree with, the -e form is used for the situation at large: hodiaŭ estas malvarme.

phrases.e: In January and February it snows

units.title: GETTING AROUND
units.subtitle: Places in a town, which way to go and how to get there

tips.h: -n on a place means going there
tips.b: al la urbo and la urbon both express movement toward. After a verb of motion a bare place word with -n names the destination, and without -n it names where one already is.

tips.h: Naming a shop by what it sells
tips.b: -ej- attached to a trade root names its premises: vendi to sell gives vendejo a shop, pano gives panejo a bakery, preĝi to pray gives preĝejo a church.

phrases.t: La muzeo estas en la urbo
phrases.e: The museum is in the city
phrases.ipa: la mu.ˈze.o ˈes.tas en la ˈur.bo

tips.b: An adverb of place adds -n for movement toward it: dekstre on the right gives dekstren to the right, tie there gives tien to there, hejme at home gives hejmen homeward.
eg: on the right / to the right

tips.h: al and de need no accusative
tips.b: al already means toward and de already means away from, so the noun after them stays plain. The accusative follows only a preposition that states a position, such as en, sur or sub.

tips.h: ĉi- and i- complete the table
tips.b: Beside ki-, ti- and neni- stand ĉi- for every and i- for some: ĉie everywhere and ie somewhere, ĉiam always and iam sometime, ĉio everything and io something.

phrases.t: La kato estas sub la tablo
phrases.e: The cat is under the table
phrases.ipa: la ˈka.to ˈes.tas sub la ˈta.blo

phrases.t: La lampo estas super la lito
phrases.e: The lamp is above the bed
phrases.ipa: la ˈlam.po ˈes.tas ˈsu.per la ˈli.to

phrases.t: La parko estas apud la muzeo
phrases.e: The park is beside the museum
phrases.ipa: la ˈpar.ko ˈes.tas ˈa.pud la mu.ˈze.o

tips.b: The preposition per states the instrument or the means by which something is done: per trajno by train, per aŭto by car, per krajono with a pencil.

tips.h: Compounds name what a place is for
tips.b: A place of transport is usually two roots, and the final one carries the ending: stacidomo is a station building and flughaveno a flight harbour.

phrases.t: La trajno haltas en la stacidomo
phrases.e: The train stops at the station
phrases.ipa: la ˈtraj.no ˈhal.tas en la sta.t͡si.ˈdo.mo

tips.b: The future tense ends in -os for every subject alike: mi vojaĝos, ni vojaĝos, ili vojaĝos. There is no separate form for will and shall.
A preposition used as a prefix fixes the direction of a verb: al-veni to arrive, for-iri to go away, en-iri to enter, el-iri to go out.

units.title: PEOPLE
units.subtitle: Feeling, the body, being ill and describing a person

tips.b: The suffix -ec- turns a description into the abstract quality: bela beautiful gives beleco beauty, amiko friend gives amikeco friendship, feliĉa gives feliĉeco happiness.

tips.h: ŝati takes an object, plaĉi a subject
tips.b: ŝati means to like and takes the thing liked as its object: mi ŝatas kafon. plaĉi turns the sentence round, so the thing liked becomes the subject: kafo plaĉas al mi.

tips.h: la, not a possessive, for the body
tips.b: A body part belonging to the subject usually takes la rather than a possessive: mi lavas la manojn, I wash my hands. A possessive appears only where the owner would otherwise be unclear.
A pair of body parts is an ordinary plural: la okuloj, la manoj. Any adjective with it takes -j, and both words take -n when they are the object.

tips.h: -u gives an order or a request
tips.b: The ending -u forms the imperative, and it serves every subject: venu come, ni iru let us go, li venu have him come. bonvolu before an infinitive turns an order into a request.

tips.h: -ul- names a person by a trait
tips.b: The suffix -ul- makes a person marked by the root: juna young gives junulo a youth, malsana ill gives malsanulo a patient, riĉa gives riĉulo a rich person.
The suffix -ist- names the person who does the root as a trade: kuraci to treat gives kuracisto doctor, instrui to teach gives instruisto teacher, kanti gives kantisto singer.
ĉiu each, ĉio everything, ĉie everywhere, ĉiam always, ĉies everyone's. ĉiu and ĉio take -n as objects, and ĉiu takes -j for a plural, ĉiuj homoj meaning all people.
A verb root with -ant- and an adjective ending describes the doer in the act: la kuranta hundo, the running dog. -int- gives what has done and -ont- what is about to do.

phrases.e: The rich man is not happy

units.title: WORK AND SCHOOL
units.subtitle: The classroom, jobs, the numbers past ten and paying

tips.b: The active participle -ant- with a noun ending names whoever is performing the action now: lerni gives lernanto a learner, instrui gives instruanto the one teaching. -ist- names it as a trade instead.
A verb root with -o names the act or its result: labori to work gives laboro work, demandi to ask gives demando a question, respondi gives respondo an answer.

phrases.t: La lernantoj studas en la lernejo
phrases.ipa: la ler.ˈnan.toj ˈstu.das en la ler.ˈne.jo

tips.b: kiel before a bare noun says in what capacity a person acts: mi laboras kiel kuiristo, I work as a cook. The noun after it takes no article and no -n.
One trade root yields both the worker and the workplace: kuiri gives kuiristo a cook and kuirejo a kitchen; vendi gives vendisto a seller and vendejo a shop.

phrases.e: My father works in an office

tips.b: A multiple of ten is written as one word, dudek, tridek; a sum keeps its parts separate, dudek unu. Hundreds and thousands follow the same rule: ducent, tri mil.
A numeral takes -a for the ordinal and -e for the adverb: unu gives unua first and unue firstly, du gives dua second and due secondly. -obl- gives a multiple, so duobla is double.

phrases.e: A hundred years is a century

tips.b: A price is asked with kiom kostas and answered with a numeral and the currency. The amount is the object of kosti and takes -n.

tips.h: -er- names one piece of a mass
tips.b: The suffix -er- takes a single unit out of a mass: mono money gives monero a coin, sablo sand gives sablero a grain, neĝo gives neĝero a snowflake.

phrases.e: How much does the book cost?

units.title: OUT AND ABOUT
units.subtitle: Ordering, buying and what people do for pleasure

tips.b: An order in -u is direct: donu al mi la menuon. bonvolu before the infinitive softens it into a request, and mi petas after a phrase does the same work.

tips.h: ek- marks the start of an action
tips.b: The prefix ek- states that an action begins or happens all at once: iri to go gives ekiri to set off, vidi to see gives ekvidi to catch sight of, dormi gives ekdormi to fall asleep.

phrases.t: Bonvolu doni al mi la kalkulon
phrases.ipa: bon.ˈvo.lu ˈdo.ni al mi la kal.ˈku.lon

tips.b: The conditional ends in -us and has one form for every subject: mi aĉetus, I would buy. It is used in a wish and in both halves of an if-sentence, after se.
oni names a subject left unnamed, as English one or people: oni diras, people say. It has no plural, and its possessive is onia.

phrases.e: I look for a light bag
I would like to buy that book

phrases.t: La kliento pagas en la butiko
phrases.e: The customer pays in the store
phrases.ipa: la kli.ˈen.to ˈpa.ɡas en la bu.ˈti.ko

tips.h: ŝati and voli take an infinitive
tips.b: A verb of liking, wanting or being able is followed straight by the infinitive, with no linking word: mi ŝatas kanti, ŝi volas danci, ni povas ludi.

tips.h: -ad- turns an act into a pastime
tips.b: The suffix -ad- names an action carried on over time: kanti to sing gives kantado singing, legi to read gives legado reading, danci gives dancado dancing.

phrases.e: She likes to sing and dance

tips.h: -int- and -ont- place the doer in time
tips.b: Beside -ant-, the doer in the act, stand -int- for the one who has finished and -ont- for the one about to begin. All three take the ordinary adjective and noun endings.
si refers back to the subject of its own clause, and only in the third person: li lavas sin, he washes himself. mi and vi use their own accusative forms instead.

phrases.t: Ni ludas futbalon en la parko
phrases.e: We play football in the park
phrases.ipa: ni ˈlu.das fut.ˈba.lon en la ˈpar.ko

phrases.t: Li kuras pli rapide ol mi
phrases.e: He runs faster than I do
phrases.ipa: li ˈku.ras pli ra.ˈpi.de ol mi

units.title: THE WORLD
units.subtitle: Nature, the city, the countries and more everyday verbs

tips.b: Two roots make one noun and the second carries the meaning: sunsubiro is a sun-going-under, a sunset; terpomo an earth-apple, a potato; akvofalo a water-fall.
The prefix re- returns or repeats: veni to come gives reveni to come back, vidi to see gives revidi to see again, legi gives relegi to read once more.

phrases.t: Mi vidas la sunon kaj la lunon
phrases.e: I see the sun and the moon
phrases.ipa: mi ˈvi.das la ˈsu.non kaj la ˈlu.non

phrases.t: Ŝi kolektas florojn en la ĝardeno
phrases.e: She gathers flowers in the garden
phrases.ipa: ʃi ko.ˈlek.tas ˈflo.rojn en la d͡ʒar.ˈde.no

tips.b: A preposition also serves as a prefix on a verb and, with -e, as an adverb of its own: antaŭ before gives antaŭe in front and antaŭiri to go ahead of.
The -es forms name a possessor: kies whose, ties that one's, ĉies everyone's, nenies nobody's. They never take -j or -n, because the thing owned carries those endings.

phrases.t: La ponto estas en la centro
phrases.e: The bridge is in the centre
phrases.ipa: la ˈpon.to ˈes.tas en la ˈt͡sen.tro

phrases.e: My neighbour works in a café

tips.b: A country is usually the name of its people plus -io: franco a French person gives Francio, germano gives Germanio. A land named for its territory keeps its own root, as Brazilo and Nederlando do.
The suffix -an- names a member or an inhabitant: urbo gives urbano a townsman, klubo gives klubano a club member, Eŭropo gives eŭropano a European.
A language is named with the adjective of its people and the noun lingvo, or with the adjective alone: la angla lingvo, la angla. The -e form says in what language something is done.
The passive participles describe what receives the action: la libro estas legata, the book is being read; legita, already read. The one who does it follows de.

tips.h: The full tense set on one root
tips.b: One root carries every form the verb has: fari to do, faras does, faris did, faros will do, farus would do, faru do. Nothing else in the sentence changes.
ke introduces a whole clause after a verb of saying, thinking or knowing. The verb inside keeps the tense it would have had standing alone.
eg: I think that she is right
He said that he will come

phrases.e: She said that she will come
We live in a small village

phrases.t: Ĉu vi povas malfermi la fenestron?
phrases.ipa: t͡ʃu vi ˈpo.vas mal.ˈfer.mi la fe.ˈnes.tron
